{{Short description|American experimental particle physicist (1932-2012)}}
'''William J. Willis''' (15 September 1932, [[Fort Smith, Arkansas]] – 1 November 2012, [[Dobbs Ferry, New York]])<ref>biographical information, Thomson Gale 2004</ref > was an American experimental [[Particle physics|particle physic]]ist.

==Biography==
William Willis studied physics at [[Yale University]], where he received his bachelor's degree in 1954 and his PhD in 1958 with advisor [[Earle Fowler]] and dissertation related to the development of hydrogen [[bubble chamber]]s in [[Ralph P. Shutt]]'s research group. Willis was a postdoc at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] (BNL), where he observed weak decays of [[kaon]]s and [[hyperon]]s in bubble chambers. In 1961/62 he was at [[CERN]], where he was involved in experiments on weak decays of hyperons, which confirmed the [[Nicola Cabibbo|Cabibbo]] theory of weak interaction. In 1964 Willis joined the faculty of Yale University.<ref name=Obit/> From 1973 to 1991, he was at CERN, where he undertook experiments at the [[Intersecting Storage Rings|ISR]], developing novel detector concepts. He was essential for the development of the ISR's Axial Field Spectrometer, which detected the first high-pt jet events in hadronic collisions.<ref name=CERN/><ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Martinez, Mario|title=High Pt Jet Physics|eprint=hep-ex/0610036v2|year=2006 }}</ref> The approach used in the Axial Field Spectrometer became standard for hadron colliders.<ref name=CERN>[https://cds.cern.ch/record/1493559 obituary at CERN]</ref>

{{blockquote|Subsequently he turned his interest to nuclear matter under extreme conditions of temperature and density: he convinced the CERN management to adapt the [[Super Proton Synchrotron|SPS]] to the acceleration of heavy ions, including lead ions, thus opening a new field, which flourished at [[RHIC]] and now also at the LHC.<ref name=CERN/>}}

In 1991 Willis became the Eugene Higgins Professor of Physics at Columbia University. Following the failure to fund the [[Superconducting Super Collider]], he sought ways to involve US physicists in CERN's [[Large Hadron Collider|LHC]] plans, and was a member of the first US delegation to CERN in 1993. In the 2000s he was (until 2005) Project Manager in the US Department of [[ATLAS Collaboration]] at CERN's LHC.<ref name="Obit">{{cite web |title=Obituary. William (Bill) J. Willis 1932 – 2012 |url=https://physics.columbia.edu/william-bill-j-willis-1932-2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211073533/https://physics.columbia.edu/william-bill-j-willis-1932-2012 |archive-date=11 December 2013 |website=Department of Physics, Columbia University}}</ref>

From 1994 to 2010 he was assistant director of the BNL. Among other things, he supported the construction of the [[Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider|RHIC]], which went into operation in 2000, and led the technical committee for the RHIC in the 1980s. More recently, he contributed his expertise in liquid argon detectors to the planning of neutrino experiments at [[Fermilab]]'s ([[MicroBooNE]] experiment).<ref name=Obit/>

He was a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and in 2003 received the [[Panofsky Prize]] for "his leading role in the development and exploitation of innovative techniques now widely adopted in particle physics, including liquid argon calorimetry, [[Transition radiation detectors|electron identification by detection of transition radiation]], and [[hyperon]] beams."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Willis&first_nm=William&year=2003|website=American Physical Society|title=2003 W.F.H. Panofsky Prize in Experimental Particle Physics Recipient, William J. Willis}}</ref> In 1993 he was elected a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

Willis was married and had one daughter and four sons.
